section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p: This document is in Request-For-Comments release 7; it is not a definitive release.

ZapRedraw is a module capable of drawing a rectangle of text characters on screen. It originates from the text editor, Zap, but is often used in applications where a text display is required, being superior to that natively provided by RISC OS.

list.item: Redraw may be by direct screen access (henceforth DSA) where the data is poked into the screen memory or by the standard VDU redraw.
Full colour provided (with your own definable palette). Supports up to 32 bits per pixel in DSA mode and 24 bit colour in VDU mode.

DSA redraw can handle any size of bitmap characters. Special optimised code is provided for 8 pixel wide characters in all modes. Also 8 × 8 and 8 × 16 character sizes are given priority. Up to 65536 characters can be defined.
VDU redraw mode can handle any font, at any size and aspect ratio.
Support is provided for cursors.
Many extra SWIs perform all the work of creating cached bitmaps, updating them on a mode change etc. SWIs are also provided for creating palettes and other functions related to the redraw.
An example program is provided which can be used as a template.
New font handles concept allows easier handling of cached characters, mode changing, font sub-styles, and reduces DSA/VDU mode differences.

section.p: It also has the following limitations:

list.item: All characters are equally spaced. Proportional spacing is not supported.

Is a bulleted list for the DSA/VDU distinction a good way of presenting that information.
The extensions for ZapRedraw_RedrawArea are essentially entrypoints with reason codes, so could be restructured to use the entry-definition format.
Related APIs aren't linked at all

subsection.title: Pixel co-ordinates
subsection.p: Pixel co-ordinates are used wherever possible to prevent rounding errors when OS co-ordinates are not pixel aligned (these errors do mess things up).

Pixel co-ordinates are from the top left of the screen with the y axis descending. By a 'pixel' I mean a hardware pixel (this differs from an OS pixel in double-pixel emulation modes - this only crops up in the RISC OS 2 MODE 2 wimp!).

subsection.title: Character cache format (r_caddr)
subsection.p: When using VDU redraw, this should point to the name of the font to use, or be zero for the system font.

When using direct screen access, the module will expect this block to contain the bitmaps for all the characters it is asked to print. Each character has size r_cbpc so it will expect to find the bitmap for ASCII character 'n' at address char_start = (!r_caddr) + n × r_cbpc. The character definition then consists of r_charh rows of r_cbpl each so r_cbpc = r_charh × r_cbpl. NB r_cbpl need not be a multiple of 4 so this address need not be word aligned.

The format of a row is the same as that for a sprite file except there is never any left hand side wastage. Ie, the first pixel is aligned to the start of the first word. Each character is r_charw pixels wide and thus requires N = r_charw << r_bpp bits of storage. There are special cases when N is small:

item.p: If 0 < N ≤ 8 then r_cbpl = 1 and the top 8-N bits of the byte are wasted.
If 8 < N ≤ 16 then r_cbpl = 2 and the top 16-N bits of the row are wasted.
If N > 16 then r_cbpl is aligned to the next multiple of 4 bytes greater or equal to N. (eg if 16 < N ≤ 32 then r_cbpl = 4, and if 32 < N ≤ 64 then r_cbpl = 8, etc).

subsection.p: The SWI will calculate the values of r_cbpl and r_cbpc for you from a given size of character.

Only TWO colours can be used in the definition of the character. Set all foreground pixels to 1's and background pixels to 0's. Eg, in a 16 colour mode pixels will be either 1111 or 0000. Unused bits at the end of the words (or bytes) are ignored and so can contain rubbish. The real foreground and background colours are masked in at run time.
Examples:

For 8 × 8 characters at 1 bit per pixel we have 1 byte per row. Eg "E" may be cached as:
01111110 01100000 01100000 01111110 01100000 01100000 01111110 00000000

If it was in a 16 colour mode then there would be one word per row and the first rows would be:
00001111111111111111111111110000 00001111111100000000000000000000
In general you have:
Word 0 Word (N/4)-1
In practice you first cache the font at one bit per pixel (eg use ) and then convert it to 'n' bits per pixel (for the current mode) by use of .

Although I have said that the foreground colour must be all 1's and the background all 0's this is not strictly true. The data poked into the screen memory is (foreground mask AND bitmap) OR (background mask BIC bitmap). Thus if you have a foreground mask of &hex;FFFFFFFF and a background mask of 0 then the bitmap will be poked directly into the screen so can have any format you like (though character merging and several other features may not work properly). This idea can be used in conjunction with to create a fast redraw mode for anti aliased fonts (as used in Zap).

subsection.title: Format of text to display (r_data)
subsection.p: This block contains the text to be printed on the screen. There should be sufficient text here to redraw the specified area of the screen (given its size, the scroll offset, character sizes etc). Terminating each line with the bytes 0,2 will ensure the redraw doesn't run out of text horizontally and terminating the line list with a zero will ensure the same vertically. The value in r_data points to a list of words. The n'th word in the list is the offset (from the block data start) of the n'th line of text to be printed in the window. This list can be terminated by a 0 offset in which case all further lines will be cleared to background colour (r_bac).

The data for each line consists of a string of bytes giving the characters to print. By character number 'n' is meant the n'th (n starting from 0) bitmap in your character cache in DSA mode, or the character with code 'n' in VDU redraw mode.

The byte 0 in the data for a line introduces a control code. Bytes 1-255 just print characters n = 1-255 as normal, within the current chunk of 256 characters. The chunk is chunk 0 (characters 0-255) at the start of each line, and is changed by the control codes 0,11 and 0,12, so that characters above 255 may be reached. When the chunk is C then the byte b prints character C + b (C is always a multiple of 256, so characters from 0 to &hex;FFFFFF may be reached). For a character cache which you supply, there is only chunk 0 and the control code 0,3 may be used to reach the characters above 255. Characters which are not defined are drawn using the null glyph. The characters 0-31 and the character &hex;7F are not normally letters; Zap treats these specially - see below.
The currently defined control sequences are:

subsection.p: Where a control code takes a sub-style S, it is a sub-style. In DSA mode with a font handle, ZapRedraw changes the sub-style for you; the change is also reported to the extension routine, if there is one. With a character cache you supply, sub-style changes can only be performed by an extension routine.

Note that sequences with codes 0, 3, 4 and 8 evaluate to one 'screen printable character', codes 1, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 to none, and code 2 to as many as is required. Thus it is not a simple matter to calculate the start of the n'th actual printable character given a string containing control codes as above. The SWI does this for you.

In DSA mode with a character cache you supply, character 'n' just looks up the cached character at address r_caddr + n × r_cbpc. Usually the bitmaps will correspond to the VDU list below so that character &hex;20 will be the bitmap for a space etc. If r_caddr is a font handle then ZapRedraw looks up the character in the font, and uses the font's null glyph for characters which the font does not define. The cursor characters &hex;100-&hex;105 (used by the 0,8 control code) are always available in a font handle, and ZapRedraw generates the control characters 0-&hex;1F and the null glyph if the font does not contain them.

ZapRedraw supports sixteen sub-styles, in both VDU and DSA redraw modes, using the same convention in both. The sub-style number is a byte S in which bit 0 means strikethrough, bit 5 bold, bit 6 italic and bit 7 underlined. The sub-style at the start of the line is the bottom 8 bits of r_caddr when it is a font handle, and the control codes 0,9 and 0,10 change it during the line. See Sub-styles for how each mode renders them.

subsection.title: Sub-styles
subsection.p: A sub-style is a variation of the base font. The sub-style number S is a byte in which:

value-table.value: Strikethrough
Bold
Italic
Underlined

subsection.p: The other bits are ignored when selecting a font (except that, in DSA mode, bit 4 has the same effect as bit 0). uses bit 3 of the sub-style list to mean inverse video, and swaps the foreground and background colours while it is set.

In DSA mode each sub-style has its own bitmaps. ZapRedraw looks for a file in the font directory whose name is made up of the letters of the sub-style (see the description of font files); if the exact combination is not present, it falls back to the nearest combination which is, and finally the base font.

In VDU mode the font is a Font Manager font. If r_flags bit 3 is set, ZapRedraw looks for the variants of the font named by appending .Bold, .Oblique (or .Italic), and .Bold.Oblique (or .Bold.Italic) to the font name; where the font name already ends in a style, the final component is replaced. The bold and italic bits (5 and 6) select between the four fonts found. Strikethrough and underline are drawn as lines by ZapRedraw. Rendering of the variants has some technical difficulties, because they tend to have different bounding boxes from the default font at the same point size and aspect ratio; no attempt is made to compensate for this.

subsection.title: Format of palette data (r_palette)
subsection.p: All colours are specified as offsets in the palette table. Thus if you set r_for to 1 then the module will look up the word at offset 4*1 in the palette table when it comes to printing a character.

category.title: DSA Mode
category.p: The palette consists of a list of words giving the colour 'mask' to use for this colour. The mask is duplicated to fill the word out. For example, in a 16 colour mode, the mask &hex;AAAAAAAA would stand for actual screen colour 10. The table:
would cause 3 to be poked into the screen when in zap colour 0, 6 when in zap colour 1 etc. The masks will usually correspond to the wimp colours. The SWI is provided to set them up.
The actual value poked into the screen is: (Foreground mask AND bitmap) OR (Background mask BIC bitmap) where the bitmap is as specified in r_caddr.

category.title: VDU Mode
category.p: The palette consists of a list of words giving the 24 bit colour required. The word is in the form of a standard palette entry. Ie, &hex;BBGGRRxx where &hex;BB is the amount of blue etc. These will usually be set up by reading the wimp palette. The SWI will do this for you. ColourTrans calls will be used during the redraw to find the closest available GCOL colour.

subsection.title: Font handles
subsection.p: Font handles are a concept introduced in ZapRedraw 0.40. They make the process of loading and caching fonts much easier, and they also allow transparent access to font sub-styles in DSA mode in the same manner as in VDU mode. To initialise your font, pass the font name (eg 08x16.System) to , and place the returned font handle in r_caddr. To find the size of the font, the call is provided. When you have finished with the font, you should call .
Font handles take the form &hex;HHHHHHSS

HHHHHH is the font handle proper (a number from 1 to 32), and SS is the sub-style. Thus the lower 8 bits of r_caddr are the initial font sub-style to use at the start of the line. They have the same effect as r_for and r_bac. 0,9 and 0,10 control codes may be used to change sub-style during the line. Any value of r_caddr below &hex;8000 is taken to be a font handle; larger values are the addresses of a character cache or font name which you provide.
When r_caddr is a font handle, ZapRedraw does the following for you:

item.p: It loads the font on demand, converts the bitmaps to the number of bits per pixel in r_bpp, and converts them again when r_bpp changes, so you do not need to cache the characters yourself. In modes with 32 bits per pixel the 1 bit per pixel bitmaps are plotted directly.

It sets r_charw, r_charh, r_cbpl and r_cbpc in the redraw block to match the font each time the block is used for DSA redraw. (In VDU mode the character size is that of the cell in which the font is plotted, and it is not stored in the block.)
It provides its own workspace, if r_workarea is 0.

It changes the sub-style for the control codes 0,9 and 0,10, and selects the chunk for the control codes 0,11 and 0,12. The characters above 255 which the font contains can therefore be drawn, and those it does not contain are drawn as the null glyph.
If r_flags bit 5 is set, it chooses double height mode.

subsection.p: A font handle is counted: each call to which finds an already loaded font adds a user to the handle, and each call to removes one. There are 32 handles available to all the applications which use ZapRedraw. The font data remains cached after it has no users, so that a font which is closed and then reopened is not reloaded, until the memory is needed for another font or until is used.

A font handle allocated for VDU mode may be passed directly to in DSA mode. This converts it to anti-aliased bitmaps on demand, exactly as Zap's aa-DSA mode does. The algorithm used is simple, but gives good results; it chooses an anti-aliased bitmap unless the colours of the text and its background are too similar for it to matter, when it uses a 1 bit per pixel bitmap instead, and it never uses anti-aliasing if r_flags bit 9 is set. Sub-styles are ignored.
The application should lose its handles when it has finished, before the module can be killed. ZapRedraw cannot be killed while any handle has users (see ).

subsection.title: Fonts and the font path
subsection.p: The bitmap fonts which DSA redraw uses are found along the path variable ZapFontsSource$Path. This is a comma separated list of directories, which the application !ZapFonts sets to the directories Fonts and Encodings inside it. An application which uses ZapRedraw should use !ZapFonts rather than carry its own fonts, so that the fonts are shared; !ZapFonts also sets Zap$Redraw to the location of the ZapRedraw module, which an application's !Run file can use to load the module.

A font is a file within one of the directories (or within a subdirectory of them; the names use dots to separate the levels, and are not case sensitive), such as 08x16.System for the font in the file 08x16.System. A font directory is a directory whose name is used as the font name. The file named 0 within it is the base font, and the others are its sub-styles (see Font files). If the name of a font is the name of a directory and not of a file, then the base font in it is used, and its sub-styles. A link is a small text file which refers to another font; the names of fonts are the names of the links and the fonts. The names of fonts follow the convention <width>x<height>.<name>, such as 08x16.System, though this is not enforced by the module.

The names which ZapRedraw lists in menus (see ) come from Messages files. In each directory on the path, ZapRedraw looks for the file Messagesn, where n is the number of the current territory (in decimal); if it is not there, the file Messages1 is used. This is a normal MessageTrans file in which each line
describes one font, and each line

describes one encoding. The identifier is the name by which the font or encoding is found on the path. As brackets cannot be used in the tokens, < and > are used in the identifier in their place and are converted to brackets when the identifier is read. The name is the text to show to the user in the territory; if it is empty, the identifier is used instead, and if it ends in * then that font is the default one for an ambiguous name (and the * is not part of the name). The lists are scanned when the module starts, and can be scanned again by after the path has changed. They are sorted using the territory's collation.

subsection.title: Font files
subsection.p: Font files must be of type Data (&hex;FFD) and link files of type Text (&hex;FFF). There are two formats of font file: the original format, used for fonts of up to 256 glyphs, and the format which divides fonts of up to 4 billion glyphs into chunks.

The bitmaps of the glyphs are held at one bit per pixel in the format used for the character cache of a 2 colour mode: each row of a glyph is a whole number of bytes (1 byte if the glyph is up to 8 pixels wide, 2 if up to 16 pixels wide, and otherwise the next multiple of 4 bytes), the leftmost pixel is in the least significant bit, and the rows start at the top of the glyph. Pixels which are set are in the foreground colour.
The original format is:

subsection.p: Any glyphs above 255 in the file are ignored. If the font does not start at character 0 then the glyphs for the control characters 0-&hex;1F are made from the letters (0 is the digit 0, and 1-&hex;1F are copies of &hex;41-&hex;5F). The cursor glyphs for characters &hex;7F and &hex;100-&hex;105 are always made by ZapRedraw, as is the null glyph, which is used for the characters the font does not define.

subsection.p: The chunk directory follows immediately. The glyphs are divided into chunks of up to 256 glyphs, and the directory has an entry of four words for each chunk:

offset-table.offset: The number of the first glyph of the chunk: a chunk containing the glyph &hex;2A3F has &hex;2A00 here

subsection.p: The glyph data for a chunk consists of the bitmaps of the glyphs in order. If the chunk has fewer than 256 glyphs then the data starts with a translation table of 256 bytes: for each of the 256 characters of the chunk, the table gives the number of its glyph in the data plus 1, or 0 if it is not defined. The table is not present for a chunk with all 256 glyphs. Chunk 0 must be present and have all 256 glyphs, including the glyphs for the control characters; it should use the Acorn Extended Latin 1 encoding where possible. The null glyph is a bitmap of the same size as the others; if there is none then ZapRedraw uses a dotted box. ZapRedraw loads chunk 0 when it loads the font and the other chunks the first time that they are needed.

Where a font has sub-styles, it is a directory. The file 0 is the base font, and the files for the sub-styles have names made of the letters of the styles they are for, in the order U, S, I, B: B (bold), I (italic), S (strikethrough), U (underlined), or any combination such as IB or USIB. When ZapRedraw needs a sub-style it tries the file for exactly that combination of styles. If there is none, it takes away the styles in turn and tries again: first underline, then italic, then bold, then strikethrough; then pairs of styles; then it uses the single style files if they exist; and finally the base font. Fonts directly in the font directory are not given sub-styles.

A link file contains the bytes "ZFLK" followed by 10, and then the path of the font linked to, ending in a zero byte. A link cannot refer to another link. A link may be the file 0 of a font directory, which is the base font when the directory is chosen.

subsection.title: Encodings
subsection.p: An encoding translates the character codes of text into Unicode, so that text in any of the 8 bit character sets can be displayed using a font which holds Unicode characters. Encodings are found by name along ZapFontsSource$Path, and are handled with . An encoding file is of type Data (&hex;FFD) and has the format:

offset-table.offset: The bytes "ZENC"
File format version - must be 2
Reserved (0)
Reserved (0)
256 words, one for each character code from 0 to 255, giving the Unicode character for the code, or -1 if the code is not defined

subsection.p: Two encodings are built in: UTF8 and UTF16, which are not tables and have no file. The supplied encodings are the ISO Latin character sets (Latin1 to Latin10), Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, Cyrillic, KOI8-R, Thai and Welsh.

subsection.title: Memory use, caching and mode changes
subsection.p: The font data and the converted bitmaps are held in a dynamic area named "Zap font cache" (the name is a message token, FontCache), which is created when the module starts, and which can be at most 2 megabytes. If the dynamic area cannot be created because the system does not support them (which is the case before RISC OS 3.5) then font handles cannot be used in DSA mode. The memory is returned when fonts with no users are tidied and the cache is compacted, either when a new font is needed or with .

ZapRedraw watches for the mode change service call (, &hex;46). On a mode change the sizes of the VDU fonts are read again for the new mode. The DSA fonts are converted again to the new number of bits per pixel the next time that they are used. Applications must read the screen details into the redraw block again with , and the number of bits per pixel for the cache with , after a mode change.

subsection.title: VDU redraw mode
subsection.p: In VDU redraw mode ZapRedraw draws with the operating system rather than writing the screen memory. Each line is drawn in three passes: first the backgrounds, as rectangles of each background colour (using the fast rectangle plot of if r_flags bit 4 is set, and OS_Plot otherwise); then the characters, with Font_Paint for a font and OS_WriteC for the system font; and then any merged characters and cursors. The colours of the palette entries are translated to the nearest available colours with ColourTrans.

The system font is used when the font name is 0. The characters 0-&hex;1F, &hex;7F and &hex;100-&hex;105 are drawn as described in Format of text to display by ZapRedraw, since the operating system's meaning of these characters is not the one wanted. Characters above 255 are drawn with UTF-8 text if the Font Manager supports it (Font Manager 3.40 or later); the system font characters are defined temporarily with VDU 23 in the Unicode range of the operating system, via the international service call (&hex;43), and restored afterwards.

subsection.title: ViewFinder
subsection.p: If the ViewFinder module (version 1.29 or later) is present and is in use (the system variable ViewFinder$Enable being set to a non-zero number, or ViewFinder 1.41 or later which is assumed to be active), ZapRedraw has ViewFinder draw the text and the rectangles, since ViewFinder modes cannot be written directly. This is automatic and needs nothing from the application, except that cannot be used, and returns 0 so that 1 bit per pixel caches are used.

Call to fill in the screen details, and again after each mode change.

use.p: This SWI is to help prepare the r_data field of the redraw block. It takes as input the pointer to a line of text characters, which are treated as ordinary characters (0 is not a control code). It also takes as input a pointer to a background list and a foreground list, giving the background and foreground colours of each character separately. The output is a line of the format required by r_data with control codes changing the colours, sub-style and chunk, and specifying the line end. Control codes in the input string can have their colour set automatically by setting R0 to the colour.
The width of the input characters is 8 bits unless r_flags bit 10 (16 bits) or bit 11 (32 bits) is set. The characters are then translated according to the encoding in r_encoding, if there is one:

list.item: If the encoding is a table (as found by for an encoding such as Latin1) then 8 bit input characters are looked up in the table to give Unicode characters. Table entries of -1 give the character &hex;FFFF.

use.p: Whenever the character is not within the current chunk, a 0,11 or 0,12 control code is generated to change chunk. The output is that of a single line, so the chunk is 0 at the end. The buffer must be large enough for the output. For text of 8 bit characters with no encoding, 6 × R5 + 16 bytes are sufficient (a colour change, a 0 changed to 0,0, and the terminator). Where chunk changes and sub-styles can be generated, each character may need up to 11 bytes (0,10,f,b,S then 0,12,l,h then the character as 0,0), so allow 11 bytes for every character plus 16.

swi-definition.name: ZapRedraw_FindFont
swi-definition.description: Finds a font and returns a font handle.

entry.register-use: Pointer to font name, or 0 for system font.

Flags:
Set if VDU mode; clear for DSA mode. Set if R4 points to a reduction block. This applies to VDU mode only; it is ignored in DSA mode. Reserved - set to 0
X size (in points × 16). Only applicable in VDU mode.
Aspect ratio (Y / X × 100), or 0 for the same as the X size. Only applicable in VDU mode.
Pointer to reduction block. Only applicable in VDU mode.

use.p: This finds a font and returns a font handle which should be placed in r_caddr. All of the font's substyles are opened as well, if available. The font handle has the form &hex;HHHHHH00 where HHHHHH is a number from 1 to 32; the bottom byte is the sub-style, and you may set it to the initial sub-style for the line before using the handle in r_caddr. Any value below &hex;8000 in r_caddr is a font handle; larger values are the addresses of character caches or font names.

If the font has already been found with the same name (and, in VDU mode, the same size, aspect ratio and reduction block) then the same handle is returned, and the number of users of the handle is increased. Each call to FindFont must therefore be balanced by one call to . Creating a new handle also discards the data for any fonts which have no users, to free memory.

DSA mode: the font name is either a font as it appears in the ZapFonts directory, eg 08x16.System, or a complete path name of a font file or an application-specific font directory (in which case it need not be on ZapFontsSource$Path). It may also be a font identifier of the form returned by . If the name is the name of a directory then the file 0 in it is the base font, and the other files are its sub-styles. If the name is a link file, the font linked to is used. See the description of font files for details of the files. The font is loaded on demand, in the format required by the screen mode in r_bpp at the time it is used; the call itself only needs to find the font. An unusable font gives the errors "Font '%0' not found", "Font file corrupt" or "Invalid font link file". RISC OS 3.5 or later is required, because the data is held in a dynamic area; before that the call returns the error "Font handles require RISC OS 3.50 or later".

VDU mode: the font name is the Font Manager identifier of a font. If R0 is 0 then the system font is used, and the sizes are ignored. Otherwise R2 and R3 give the size at which to plot the font, as for Font_FindFont. The size of a character cell is taken from the bounding box of the characters 0-9, A-Z and a-z of the font, converted into pixels. In VDU mode, R4 may optionally point to a reduction block which allows the cell size to be fine-tuned. The block has the following form:

value-table.value: Left reduction
Top reduction
Right reduction
Bottom reduction

use.p: All values are in pixels, and are signed integers. In general, the values in this block will all be 0, so you may omit it. The system font is treated as being 8 pixels wide and 16 pixels high (8 pixels high if there are 4 or more OS units to a pixel vertically).

The handle is shared between VDU mode and DSA mode redraws as far as the font data is concerned: a handle found in VDU mode may also be used in DSA mode, when ZapRedraw converts the font to anti-aliased bitmaps on demand (unless the r_flags bit 9 asks it not to). A handle found in DSA mode cannot be used in VDU mode (this gives the error "Attempt to use a DSA font in VDU mode").
There are 32 font handles. If they are all in use the error "No more font handles" is returned.

Reason code:
Find an encoding. R1 = pointer to the encoding identifier. Returns R0 = encoding handle. Lose an encoding. R1 = encoding handle. Read the translation table. R1 = encoding handle. Returns R0 = pointer to the table.
Depends on the reason code - see above

exit.register-use: Depends on the reason code - see above

use.p: An encoding translates the character codes of a piece of text into Unicode characters. can use an encoding to translate text, and thereby display text in other character sets in fonts which contain the Unicode characters.

Reason code 0 finds an encoding by its identifier, as returned by , or by its name, such as Latin2. The encoding is loaded from the file of that name found along ZapFontsSource$Path if it is not already loaded, and the number of users of the handle is increased. The names UTF8 and UTF16 give special handles which require no file. Up to 16 encodings can be loaded at once.
Reason code 1 reduces the number of users of an encoding by one. Encodings without users are freed when space is needed and when the module is finished.

Reason code 2 returns a pointer to the translation table of an encoding. It is a table of 256 words, one for each 8 bit character code, giving the Unicode character or -1 if the character is not defined. For the special UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings, which are not tables, it returns 1 for UTF-8 and 2 for UTF-16. The table is valid until the encoding is lost.

Handles for tables are numbers from 1 to 16. The special handles for UTF-8 and UTF-16 are &hex;40000001 and &hex;40000002. An unknown reason code gives the error "Unknown ZapRedraw_Encoding reason code" (error number 0); an invalid handle gives "Invalid encoding handle".

subsection.title: Debugging commands
subsection.p: Builds of ZapRedraw made for debugging also have the commands ZapFontDescribe (describes the font blocks, encodings and free memory of the cache), ZapFontDie (forgets all font handles without freeing their memory, so that the module can be killed) and ZapFontDebug (prints an internal variable), and profiling builds also have ZapFontProfile. These are only present in debugging builds of ZapRedraw, are subject to change, and should not be relied on.

section.title: Extension routines to ZapRedraw_RedrawArea
section.p: The extension routine is provided so you can trap unknown control codes and add extra functionality to the ones that exist. For example, you may wish to change font on a colour change. Zap's fast font redraw mode does this. If you provide an extension routine then on entry to it R0 = reason code, R12 = your private word and:
On exit, you may corrupt R0 and R12 and alter the registers mentioned (EXCEPT R1!) to new (sensible) values.
All registers are reset at the start of a new raster line.
You must not alter the redraw block itself.
You CANNOT return errors from an extension call.
